Who sets and collects property tax

Property tax in South Carolina is run locally, with help from the state Department of Revenue. About two-thirds of county-levied property taxes support public education. Your county assessor values the house, the auditor and treasurer handle the bill, and school and city levies ride on the same notice.

The rules in this guide come from the state code, while rates, office hours and payment options come from your county. Call the county treasurer before you finalize a sale date.

Assessment ratios

The state taxes a percentage of fair market value, and the percentage depends on how the property is used (SC Code 12-43-220).

  • Owner-occupied legal residence, up to five contiguous acres: 4% (12-43-220(c))
  • Other real property not otherwise provided for: 6% (12-43-220(e))
  • Agricultural real property of qualifying individuals and partnerships: 4% (12-43-220(d)(1))
  • Manufacturing and utility property: 10.5% (12-43-220(a)(1))

A rental house or second home falls on the 6% line, so owner-occupants and investors get different bills on similar values.

Reappraisal every fifth year

Each county must appraise and equalize property once every fifth year (12-43-217). Valuation is to be complete by the end of December of the fourth year, with taxpayers notified of value or classification changes of $1,000 or more. New values are assessed in the fifth year.

A county may postpone putting revised values into effect by ordinance, for no more than one property tax year. If you plan to sell, find out which year your county is in. A reassessment year can move the bill your buyer inherits.

Due dates and penalties

Payment window: September 30 through January 15 after assessment (SC Code 12-45-70). Penalties begin after the later of January 16 or 30 days after notices are mailed (12-45-180(A)).

A county may allow installment payments by ordinance. Taxpayers elect in writing between December 1 and January 15, and five installments of 16 2/3% fall on February 15, April 15, June 15, August 15 and October 15 (12-45-75). Taxes paid through escrow are excluded.

How to appeal your assessment

Send the assessor a written notice of objection within 90 days of the mailing date on your assessment notice (SC Code 12-60-2510). In years with no notice, an appeal may be made in writing at any time. Timing decides the year: file before the first penalty date and it counts for that tax year, file after and it counts for the next.

  1. Notice of objection to the assessor, or a written request to meet, within the 90 days.
  2. Conference with the assessor, scheduled within 30 days of the request or as soon after as practical (12-60-2520).
  3. Then a written protest, filed within 30 days of the conference.
  4. County board of assessment appeals, 30 days after the assessor responds (12-60-2530).
  5. Last stop: a contested case hearing at the Administrative Law Court, requested within 30 days of the board's written decision (12-60-2540).

If an appeal is still open on December 31 of the tax year, the assessment is adjusted to 80% of the protested amount for payment purposes, with interest settled afterward (12-60-2550).

Homestead exemption for owners 65 and older

The first $50,000 of the dwelling's fair market value comes off the bill for owners who are 65 by December 31, or who are disabled or legally blind, and have lived in the state at least a year (SC Code 12-37-250). It reaches county, municipal, school and special assessment real estate taxes alike. The application goes in before July 16 of the tax year.

For sellers the point is simple: a buyer who is not eligible will not carry the same exemption.

What happens to the 4% rate when you sell

The 4% legal residence rate stays behind with the seller. Whoever claims it for the first time must apply before that year's first penalty date. When ownership changes, the former owner must notify the assessor within six months and the new owner files a new application (12-43-220(c)(2)(vi)). The cost of staying silent is steep: a penalty of 100% of the tax paid, plus interest at one-half of one percent per month (12-43-220(c)(2)(vii)(A)).

If the buyer will live there, the application should go in quickly. A buyer who rents it out lands on the 6% ratio.

When unpaid taxes lead to a county sale

Delinquent notices go out on April 1 or as soon after as practicable, and the property is advertised once a week for three consecutive weeks (SC Code 12-51-40). The county sells at public auction, and the high bidder must pay everything that day.

The taxpayer in default, a grantee, or a mortgage or judgment creditor can redeem for twelve months after the sale (12-51-90). The bid carries interest that rises each quarter: 3% for months one to three, 6% for four to six, 9% for seven to nine and 12% for ten to twelve. Notice is mailed neither more than 45 days nor less than 20 days before the redemption period ends (12-51-120).

On redemption, the officer cancels the sale in the tax sale book, and the purchaser is mailed a notice to return the receipt for a refund of the price plus interest (12-51-100). After a tax deed is issued, the delinquent tax collector notifies the defaulting taxpayer and the owner of record of any excess due (12-51-60). That excess is money left after taxes, penalties and costs.

An owner who thinks a sale is coming should call the county delinquent tax office early. Selling before the auction avoids the twelve-month clock entirely.

Selling mid-year

If property changes hands after assessment, the new owner may apply before a tax execution sale, and the auditor estimates the share of tax owed on the portion acquired (12-45-140). Paying that share discharges the property from those taxes. Penalties must be waived when a house transferred mid-year, the notice went to the prior owner and the new owner got no timely notice (12-45-180(B)).

The closing agent usually settles that year's tax at the table. Tell your closing attorney about any unpaid prior-year bills so they show on the payoff list. Back taxes do not always block a cash closing, because the payoff comes out of what you receive.

Before listing, a seller can pull the latest tax bill, confirm with the treasurer whether the prior year is paid, and check whether an appeal is still open. If an appeal is pending, tell the closing attorney, because the buyer will want to know which assessment the payoff was based on.

The treasurer collects only what has been entered on the county tax duplicate or ordered by the auditor (12-45-60), so the bill your closing agent pulls should match the duplicate. City or town taxes get the same relief as county taxes when a new owner pays a proportionate share (12-45-170). If land moves from one county to another by annexation, taxes are prorated between the two counties for that year (12-45-390).

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Exemptions for builders and small businesses

South Carolina exempts 100% of the improvement value of newly constructed detached single-family homes offered for sale, for the period set out in 12-37-220(B)(51). It also exempts the first $10,000 of net depreciated value of business personal property for small businesses (12-37-220(B)(54)).

These exemptions are narrow and carry conditions. An investor rehabbing an older house should not assume the new-construction exemption applies. The county auditor can tell you.

Frequently asked questions

When are South Carolina property taxes due?

The payment window runs September 30 to January 15 after assessment. Penalties start after the later of January 16 or 30 days after notices are mailed, beginning at 3% (SC Code 12-45-70, 12-45-180).

How long do I have to appeal my property assessment?

Ninety days, counted from the date the assessor mails the notice. In years without a notice you may appeal in writing at any time (12-60-2510).

Do I pay while an appeal is pending?

Yes. If the appeal is unresolved on December 31, the assessment is adjusted to 80% of the protested amount for payment, with a correction and interest afterward (12-60-2550).

Can I sell a house with back property taxes?

Yes. The unpaid tax and penalties are typically paid from sale proceeds at closing. The county treasurer can quote today's payoff.

How long can a delinquent tax sale be redeemed?

Twelve months from the sale date, with interest on the bid that steps up from 3% to 12% (12-51-90).

What the homestead exemption does

S.C. Code 12-37-250 wipes the first $50,000 of a home's fair market value off the county, municipal, school and special assessment real estate tax bill. Eligibility turns on age, total and permanent disability, or legal blindness, starting at 65.

This is a property tax break on the home. It does not protect the house from creditors, and it does not freeze the value. The state revenue department treats it as a complete exemption on that first slice of value for your legal residence, and the county auditor handles the paperwork.

Who qualifies

Qualifying takes a trigger (age, disability or blindness) and the right kind of title to the dwelling.

  • Age: a South Carolina resident for at least one year who turned 65 on or before December 31.
  • Disability: someone classified as totally and permanently disabled by a state or federal agency. A person without that classification can ask the state Vocational Rehabilitation agency to evaluate the claim.
  • Blindness: a person who is legally blind as defined in Section 43-25-20.
  • Title: the owner needs complete fee simple title or a life estate. Life estates created by will count.

A home owned jointly by spouses qualifies when either spouse meets the test before January 1 of the tax year and the one-year residency requirement is met. The statute defines permanent and total disability as being unable to do substantial gainful work because of a medically determinable impairment that lasts, or is expected to last, at least 12 continuous months or ends in death.

How and when to apply

File a written application with the county auditor ahead of July 16 of the tax year. An application filed after July 15 normally applies to the next year, with one exception for filings made before the first penalty date.

There are three routes: in person at the auditor's office, by mail with proof of age, disability or blindness, or online where the auditor can check official records. If you never apply, you give up the exemption for that year. The individual form is PT-401I. Processing runs 10 to 12 weeks, and MyDORWAY is the fastest way to file.

Homestead exemption versus the 4 percent legal residence rate

These are separate breaks. The 4 percent legal residence assessment lowers the taxable share of value on an owner-occupied home. The homestead exemption takes the first $50,000 of value off the bill for qualifying seniors, disabled owners and blind owners.

The legal residence must be approved before a real estate exemption is granted, and that application goes through the county assessor. Under 12-43-220(c), the 4 percent ratio covers the home and up to five contiguous acres the owner occupies as a legal residence. Everything else is assessed at 6 percent.

  • The first year you claim legal residence, the application is due before the first penalty date.
  • Rent the house out for more than 72 days in a calendar year and the 4 percent rate is gone.
  • Ineligible owners, and owners who wait past six months to tell the assessor they lost eligibility, can be charged a 100 percent penalty on the tax plus one-half of one percent interest per month.

What happens to the exemption when you sell

Because it attaches to the owner's permanent home, the exemption stops at the sale. A buyer does not step into it. The statute defines the dwelling place as the applicant's permanent home and legal residence.

A seller who moves within South Carolina can claim the exemption on the new residence. A surviving spouse who moves must give the auditor the new address. A surviving spouse can also keep the exemption on the current home by taking complete fee simple title or a life estate within nine months of the death, and it continues while the spouse stays unmarried and uses the home as a permanent residence (12-37-250(D)).

Claiming the exemption does not trigger a reassessment. The five-year reappraisal cycle in 12-43-217 runs on its own schedule, and a county may postpone new values by one tax year.

Taxes at closing

Real estate taxes are billed a year behind and are due between September 30 and January 15, so the closing statement usually splits the year between buyer and seller. Pay late and the bill grows: 3 percent once January 15 passes, a further 7 percent after February 2, and a further 5 percent after March 17 (12-45-70 and 12-45-180).

If title changes after assessment, the new owner can ask the auditor to apportion the taxes and costs owed by the original owner before any tax-execution sale (12-45-140). When title moves during the year and the notice went to the prior owner, the treasurer must waive penalties if the current owner never received a timely notice (12-45-180(B)).

Filing the deed carries a fee of $1.85 for each $500 of value, split $1.30 state and $0.55 county (12-24-10). Expect the seller to pay it (12-24-20). Confirm the figures with your closing attorney and the county office. Ask the auditor to tell you in writing what is still owed for the year, and carry that number to the closing table. If you are moving, give the auditor your new address so the exemption on the new home can be set up without a gap.

Other exemptions for owners in special situations

Several other exemptions exist, each with its own rules and form.

  • Disabled veteran: a dwelling with a lot not exceeding five acres.
  • Paraplegic or hemiplegic person: a dwelling and lot up to one acre.
  • Medal of Honor or former prisoner of war recipient: a dwelling and lot up to one acre.
  • Disabled law enforcement officer or firefighter with a service-connected disability: a dwelling with a lot not exceeding five acres.

These come from 12-37-220(B). Ask your county auditor which one fits before you list the home, since the right exemption can lower the carrying cost while you wait to sell.

Mobile homes and shared ownership

An owner of a mobile home on leased land may receive the exemption against personal property taxes under the same procedures. The same owner cannot receive both the real and the personal property exemption in one year (12-37-250(B)).

An owner-lessee who will own the home when the lease ends qualifies as though holding fee simple or a life estate. A part owner gets the owned percentage of the full exemption, with ownership under 5 percent treated as 5 percent, and the exemption cannot exceed the value of that interest (12-37-250(J)). Heirs who inherit a share of a parent's home should check this before a sale.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the South Carolina homestead exemption?

Your dwelling place's first $50,000 of fair market value comes off the county, municipal, school and special assessment real estate tax bill (S.C. Code 12-37-250(A)(1)).

What age do you have to be?

Age 65 by December 31 and a year of South Carolina residency are required. The age test does not apply to owners who are totally and permanently disabled or legally blind.

When is the application deadline?

Written applications must be made before July 16 of the tax year. A later application generally takes effect the following year.

Does a buyer keep my homestead exemption?

No. The exemption belongs to the applicant's permanent home and legal residence, so a buyer must qualify on their own and apply to the county auditor.

Does the exemption apply to a rental?

No. It only covers the owner's permanent residence, and renting the home for more than 72 days in a calendar year also costs you the 4 percent legal residence rate.

Estate tax in South Carolina

The state levies no estate tax on anyone who died on or after January 1, 2005, and the Department of Revenue says so directly. For an heir, that means no state estate tax return stands between you and a closing on an inherited house.

The federal estate tax runs on its own system. The federal filing line is $13,990,000 for a 2025 death and $15,000,000 for a 2026 death, tested against the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption. If a different state death tax question comes up, ask the Department of Revenue or a probate attorney.

When a federal return matters for a house

Only large estates must file a federal return, so most South Carolina families selling an inherited house will not. Simpler estates made up of cash, publicly traded securities, easily valued assets or jointly held property generally do not need to file.

Some estates file anyway. Since January 1, 2011, a decedent's estate may elect to pass any unused exemption to a surviving spouse, and the election is made on a timely filed estate tax return.

Income tax the estate may owe after a sale

The estate itself can owe income tax, and it reports on the SC1041 fiduciary return. A resident estate or trust must file if it has to file a federal fiduciary return, has any South Carolina taxable income, or has a nonresident beneficiary.

Other triggers include gross income of $600 or more, or any trust with taxable income. Nonresident estates and trusts must file when they have income or gain from South Carolina sources.

  • Both the return and the money are due on the 15th of the fourth month after year end.
  • Filing extensions run up to five and a half months, but there is no extension of time to pay.
  • Estates and trusts generally must withhold on South Carolina income distributed to nonresident beneficiaries.
  • A liability of $15,000 or more per filing period must be filed and paid electronically.

A house sale can create a gain that flows through this return. Estates and trusts may use the 44 percent capital gain deduction, which cuts the taxable amount.

Who can sell an inherited house?

The personal representative can sell, once the probate court appoints one. Under S.C. Code Section 62-3-701, a representative's duties and powers begin on appointment.

Section 62-3-715 lets a personal representative who acts reasonably for interested persons acquire or dispose of an asset, land included, at public or private sale, and sell, mortgage or lease estate real property for cash or credit. A contrary will or court order overrides those powers, and so does Section 62-3-711(b).

That subsection bars selling real property unless Section 62-3-911, the court procedures starting at Section 62-3-1301, or the will allows it. Read the will first. A sale power written into it can change which court steps you need.

Buyers are protected. Under Section 62-3-910, someone who pays value to a personal representative acting under a will's sale authority takes title free of the rights of heirs, devisees and other interested persons. The same protection covers a purchaser from a distributee holding a deed of distribution.

Probate deadlines that set the sale timeline

Creditor and contest periods set the clock, and several run for eight months or one year. Knowing these dates helps you plan a closing.

  • Inventory: the personal representative files an inventory and appraisement within ninety days of appointment, listing probate property at fair market value on the date of death.
  • Creditor notice: notice runs once a week for three weeks in a county newspaper, asking creditors to present claims within eight months after first publication (Section 62-3-801).
  • Outside limit: claims that arose before death are barred unless presented by the earlier of one year after death or the notice period (Section 62-3-803).
  • Contesting informal probate: a contest may be filed within eight months of informal probate or one year after death, whichever is later (Section 62-3-108).

Liens are different: a claim secured by estate property survives those limits, so a mortgage or tax lien stays with the house until closing pays it. Section 62-3-909 also requires a distributee who received property improperly to return it. Settle the estate carefully before heirs split the proceeds.

Closing costs on an inherited house sale

Recording a deed costs $1.85 for every $500 of value: $1.30 goes to the state and $0.55 to the county. The grantor is generally liable, with the buyer liable second.

Exempt deeds include corrective or quitclaim deeds that only confirm title already vested for no consideration, plus deeds in lieu of foreclosure to the mortgagee. A deed from a personal representative is not among them, so plan to pay the fee unless an attorney finds an exception.

The real property tax bill is the other bill that follows the house. Sumter County's Treasurer, for one, sends notices each October, bills one year in arrears, and sets January 15 as the payment date before penalties begin. Your own county's treasurer can give you the local calendar.

Problems heirs run into with the house

Heirs often carry an empty house while probate runs. Taxes, insurance and utilities keep coming, and so do repair needs. Section 62-3-703 asks the personal representative to settle and distribute the estate as expeditiously as is consistent with the estate's best interests, so a slow, costly carry gives the representative reason to move.

  • Several heirs who disagree on whether to keep or sell
  • Heirs living out of state who cannot visit the property
  • A house with deferred repairs the estate cannot fund
  • A tenant in a rental the decedent owned
  • Unpaid taxes or liens that must clear at closing

We buy houses as-is, including inherited properties, and we work with the personal representative's attorney on the paperwork. A written offer lets the heirs weigh a cash sale against a listing that would first need repairs and cleanout.

Before accepting any offer, confirm the personal representative has been appointed and has authority to sign. The closing attorney will ask for proof, so have the court's appointment papers ready.

Frequently asked questions

Does South Carolina have an inheritance tax?

No estate tax applies to South Carolina deaths from January 1, 2005 onward. For any other state death tax question, check with the Department of Revenue or a probate attorney.

How much can an estate be worth before the federal estate tax applies?

Federal returns are required above $15,000,000 for a 2026 death and $13,990,000 for a 2025 death.

Can an heir sell the house before probate ends?

Only the personal representative can sign for the estate, and those powers start when the court appoints them. Section 62-3-711(b) restricts selling real property unless Section 62-3-911, the court procedures starting at Section 62-3-1301, or the will authorizes it.

How long do creditors have to make claims against an estate?

Notice is published once a week for three weeks and asks creditors to file within eight months of first publication. Claims arising before death are barred after one year from death, or sooner for creditors given notice.

Who files the estate's income tax return?

The fiduciary files Form SC1041 when the estate has South Carolina taxable income, gross income of $600 or more, or a nonresident beneficiary. The return and payment are due the 15th day of the fourth month after the tax year ends.

The eviction path from notice to writ

A landlord here ends a tenancy with written notice, then asks a magistrate for a rule to show cause. Only a court-issued writ allows the tenant to be removed. Changing locks or shutting off water to speed things up is not allowed.

Two statutes drive the process: Chapter 40 of Title 27, the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and Chapter 37 of Title 27 on ejectment of tenants. The first decides when a lease can end. The second lays out the court steps. If you own a rented house and are thinking of selling, find out where your tenant sits on this path. That position affects the price a buyer offers and the date you can hand over keys.

Notice before the case is filed

The reason sets the notice: five days for unpaid rent, fourteen days for most other lease breaches, and thirty or seven days to end a periodic tenancy. Every one must be in writing.

SituationNotice or period
Rent unpaid (27-40-710(B))Five days from the due date, with written notice of nonpayment and intent to end
Other lease breach not fixed (27-40-710(A))Termination no sooner than 14 days after the tenant receives the notice
Week-to-week tenancy (27-40-770(a))At least 7 days written notice
Month-to-month tenancy (27-40-770(b))At least 30 days written notice
Response to rule to show cause (27-37-20)10 days after service

The lease can carry the nonpayment warning itself. The statute supplies the exact sentence a lease needs for the five-day window, so check your lease wording before you rely on it.

What happens in magistrate court

The landlord applies to the magistrate, who issues a rule telling the tenant to leave or come in and explain within ten days of service. A tenant who does nothing is followed by a warrant of ejectment.

Service is where many cases slow down. The rule can be served like a summons. If the home looks abandoned for 15 days or more, it may be fixed to the most visible part of the premises. If two tries fail, spaced 48 hours or more apart and at different times of day (eight hours or more apart), the papers may be posted and mailed through the clerk. Mailed service is complete ten days after mailing (27-37-30).

A tenant who shows up and contests gets a hearing as in other civil cases, and either side may ask for a jury. Build a few weeks of slack into any closing date for this reason.

  • Rent keeps accruing at the old rate while the tenant stays, and taking rent does not end the right to eject (27-37-150).
  • A judgment for the landlord leads to a writ of ejectment within five days (27-37-100).
  • A judgment for the tenant lets the tenant stay until the tenancy ends by agreement or law, or rent goes unpaid (27-37-110).

Who removes the tenant, and how fast

A constable or deputy sheriff carries out the writ and gives the occupants 24 hours to leave on their own after presenting it. Force is reserved for a deputy sheriff, never a constable, and then only by the least destructive means (27-37-160).

An ill or elderly tenant's removal may be delayed. Belongings set out on a public street can be removed after 48 hours, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and holidays, and the eviction notice must tell the tenant so (27-40-710(D)).

A tenant can appeal, but the ejectment goes forward unless an appeal bond is posted, and the appeal is dismissed if the bond is not filed within five days after service of the notice of appeal (27-37-120 and 27-37-130). The landlord can bring the action in magistrate's or circuit court without posting a bond (27-40-710(C)).

What a landlord cannot do

Cutting essential services or any other self-help to regain possession is off limits, unless the tenant abandoned, surrendered, or the tenancy properly ended (27-40-760).

Other rules protect tenants during a sale or an eviction:

  • Entry takes 24 hours notice and a reasonable hour, with emergencies excepted (27-40-530). Plan showings and inspections around that.
  • Retaliation is barred. Raising it as a defense to a rule to vacate requires written notice to the landlord within ten days of service. A landlord found retaliating can owe up to three months rent or treble damages (27-40-910).
  • Fifteen days of unexplained absence after a rent default can count as abandonment, and leftover property worth $500 or less may be disposed of on the terms in 27-40-730.

A willful holdover after the lease ends can cost the tenant up to three months periodic rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater, plus fees (27-40-770(c)).

How an eviction affects selling a rented house

You can sell with a case pending. The case does shift your timeline and who will buy. Most financed buyers want a vacant house or a clean lease, so many owners with a tenant in default look at an as-is cash sale.

Run through these before you list or sign:

  • With a valid lease in place, deposit duties travel with the sale. Once the tenant has written notice of a good-faith sale, the seller is free of later liability, yet the deposit stays the seller's duty until it moves to the buyer and the tenant hears about it (27-40-410 and 27-40-450).
  • Owner or agent contact details must stay current and bind a successor owner (27-40-420(b)). Give the buyer those details in writing.
  • A buyer who does not want the tenant can only take the house vacant once the tenancy has ended lawfully. Never promise a delivery date that rides on a court calendar you do not control.

If the tenant is current and the lease has months to run, selling subject to the lease may be simpler. If the tenant is in default or holding over, owners often sell with the tenant problem priced in.

Checks before selling a rental

Pull the lease, the rent ledger and the deposit record first. Then confirm the property tax status with the county.

A rented house is taxed differently from an owner's home. The 4 percent legal residence ratio does not apply to a residence rented for more than 72 days in a calendar year, and a property found ineligible can face a 100 percent penalty on the tax plus interest of one-half of one percent per month (12-43-220(c)). Other real property is assessed at 6 percent, which makes a rental's bill heavier.

Property taxes are payable between September 30 and January 15. Late penalties then stack: 3 percent, 7 percent more after February 2, and 5 percent more after March 17 (12-45-70 and 12-45-180). Ask the county auditor and treasurer for the current year's figures before closing.

Where to get help

The county magistrate's office accepts the filings, so start there. Clerks cannot advise you on the law. A landlord with a tangled case, or a tenant claiming retaliation or a holdover dispute, should talk with a South Carolina attorney.

If you want to talk through how a sale could work around a tenant situation, our team can walk through it with you at no obligation. Gather the lease, any notices served and the court papers first, so the conversation starts from the real facts.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a South Carolina eviction take?

No fixed total exists, because it depends on service and whether the tenant contests. The statutory pieces are a five-day or fourteen-day notice, a ten-day window after the rule is served, a writ within five days of a landlord win, and 24 hours to leave once the officer presents the writ.

Can a landlord lock a tenant out in South Carolina?

No. Section 27-40-760 bars self-help and willfully cutting essential services to regain possession, except for abandonment, surrender or proper termination.

How much notice ends a month-to-month lease?

Under 27-40-770(b), landlord or tenant gives thirty days or more in writing before the end date. Weekly tenancies run on a shorter fuse of seven days.

Can I sell a house while a tenant is being evicted?

Yes, nothing in the statutes bars a sale during a case. The buyer takes the property subject to the court process, and the deposit rules in 27-40-410 and 27-40-450 still cover what is owed the tenant.

What happens to a tenant's belongings after an eviction?

Belongings left on a public street can be hauled away after 48 hours, weekends and holidays excluded. Abandoned property worth $500 or less may be disposed of under 27-40-730 once its conditions are met.

What a quitclaim deed does

A quitclaim deed transfers whatever interest the signer holds, and South Carolina treats it like other deeds for signing and recording. The deed must be proved or acknowledged before it can be recorded (SC Code 30-5-30), and quitclaim and non-warranty deeds are exempt from the derivation clause rule (30-5-35).

People use them to add a spouse, clear a name after divorce or move a house into a trust. Sellers sometimes ask whether one can stand in for a regular sale deed. It does move title. A buyer's title company, though, will take a close look.

Signing requirements

The deed must be proved or acknowledged in one of the ways 30-5-30 allows, and the form in 27-7-10 contemplates two or more credible witnesses. The options are:

  • A subscribing witness swears an affidavit
  • The signing follows the Uniform Recognition of Acknowledgments Act, or the signer swears the signature is theirs
  • The grantor acknowledges the deed before an officer, with two witnesses present

A warranty clause is not required, and the form may carry other clauses the parties consider proper (27-7-20). A seal is not required if the attestation shows the parties meant the instrument to be sealed (27-7-30).

Does a quitclaim deed avoid the recording fee?

The exemption is narrow. A corrective or quitclaim deed that confirms title already vested in the grantee, with no consideration paid or to be paid, is exempt from the fee (SC Code 12-24-40(12)). If money changes hands, the exemption does not fit.

The ordinary fee is $1.85 for each $500 of value or fraction (12-24-10). The clerk or register must require an affidavit of value, and for an exempt deed the affidavit must give the reason for the exemption (12-24-70(A)(2)). A willfully false affidavit is a misdemeanor carrying a fine up to $1,000, up to a year in prison, or both (12-24-70(C)).

Transfers exempt from the fee

The exemption list in 12-24-40 is long. A few items come up in family and title situations.

TransferItem in 12-24-40
Realty valued at $100 or less(1)
Transfers where no gain or loss is recognized under IRC Section 1041(4)
Partition with no consideration beyond the interests exchanged(5)
Family partnership to partner, or family trust to beneficiary, where the only consideration is a reduced interest(9)
Corrective or quitclaim deeds confirming title already vested, with no consideration(12)
Deed in lieu of foreclosure or foreclosure deed to the mortgagee(13)

A transfer between spouses incident to divorce often falls under item 4, but the facts matter. Ask the register of deeds or clerk, or a South Carolina attorney.

Who owes the fee

The grantor is liable by default, jointly and severally if there are several, and the grantee is secondarily liable (12-24-20). For master-in-equity deeds and deeds from the federal government, a state or its subdivisions, the grantee is the liable party.

Whoever fails to pay can be penalized $50 to $500 for each failure, and a clerk who fails to collect faces that same range (12-24-120). The Department of Revenue may waive or reduce either penalty.

Joint tenancy and survivorship

Survivorship depends on specific wording. A deed naming grantees followed by the words "as joint tenants with rights of survivorship, and not as tenants in common" creates a joint tenancy (27-7-40(a)). After a joint tenant dies, the survivor may file a certified death certificate with the register of deeds, and the filing is conclusive that the tenant is deceased (27-7-40(b)).

Divorce severs a husband-and-wife joint tenancy and leaves a tenancy in common without survivorship. If a quitclaim is meant to fix title after a death or divorce, work out which of these applies before you sign.

Using a quitclaim before a sale

A quitclaim works best for cleaning up who is on title before a sale, and less well as the sale deed itself. Common uses:

  • An heir who is not the personal representative releases an interest
  • An ex-spouse signs off after divorce
  • A co-owner transfers a share to the person selling

Title companies look at the whole chain, so a quitclaim in the chain may prompt questions. When an estate is involved, a deed of distribution from the personal representative is the usual instrument instead (62-3-907).

Cash Home Buyers purchases houses as-is, even when the title is tangled. Send us what you have and we will tell you honestly whether the title needs work first.

Where to file

Take it to the register of deeds in the county where the land sits. Counties outside the 30-5-10(A) list use the clerk of court instead. Deeds executed after July 1, 1976 need the grantee's mailing address (30-5-35). The register records instruments in the order lodged and within thirty days of lodgment (30-5-90).

Checklist before you sign

Treat a quitclaim as final. The deed gives away your interest once it is delivered and recorded.

  • Confirm whether any money is changing hands, which decides whether the fee exemption applies
  • Get the signing witnessed by two people or arrange a subscribing witness affidavit (30-5-30)
  • Include the grantee's mailing address (30-5-35)
  • Prepare the affidavit stating the exemption reason if you claim one (12-24-70(A)(2))
  • Check for a mortgage, which a deed does not pay off

For a transfer into a trust or from a trust to its beneficiary, items 8 and 9 on the exemption list can matter. Moving property into a corporation, partnership or trust in exchange for an ownership interest, with no other consideration, is exempt, but transfers back out to the stockholder, partner or beneficiary are generally taxable (12-24-40(8)).

Other transfers the fee statute addresses

A few exemptions cover transfers that look like quitclaims but are different. Individual cemetery grave spaces sold by a cemetery company are exempt (12-24-40(6)), and so are contracts for the sale of timber to be cut (12-24-40(7)). Transfers to the federal government or to a state, its agencies and departments or political subdivisions, including school districts, are exempt too (12-24-40(2)).

For a house, the more relevant case is the corrective deed. If an earlier deed had a wrong legal description, a corrective deed confirming title already vested falls under item 12 when no consideration is paid.

Cost when the fee does apply

If the exemption does not fit, the fee is the same $1.85 per $500 of value or fraction as on any other deed (12-24-10), split $1.30 state and $0.55 county (12-24-90). The grantor is liable by default (12-24-20), so the person giving up the interest may owe it. Ask the register's office to run the number from the stated value before you go in.

Frequently asked questions

Is a quitclaim deed valid in South Carolina?

Yes, if it is signed and proved or acknowledged as 30-5-30 requires and then recorded. It conveys the grantor's interest without needing a warranty clause (27-7-20).

Do I pay a recording fee on a quitclaim deed?

Not if it merely confirms title already vested in the grantee with no consideration (12-24-40(12)). You still file an affidavit stating the exemption reason.

Does a quitclaim deed remove someone from a mortgage?

No. A deed does not pay off or release a loan, so talk to your lender. The deed and the loan are separate.

Can I use a quitclaim deed to sell my house?

You can record one, but buyers and title companies generally want to see the full chain of title. Ask a closing attorney which deed fits your sale.

Who pays if the fee applies?

The grantor by default, with the grantee secondarily liable (12-24-20).

When an estate needs probate

A will has to be validated by an order of informal probate or an adjudication of probate before it can prove a transfer of property or name a personal representative (SC Code 62-3-102). The main exception is the small estate affidavit, covered below. If a house sits in the decedent's name alone, the family usually needs a court-appointed personal representative before anyone can sign a deed.

There is an outer limit as well. No informal, formal testacy or appointment proceeding may start more than ten years after the death, apart from a short list of exceptions (62-3-108). After that, intestacy is treated as incontestable if nothing was filed.

Who can serve as personal representative

South Carolina ranks who gets first call on the appointment, and the person named in the will comes first. Under 62-3-203 the order runs like this:

  1. The person with priority under a probated will, including a nominee named in it
  2. A surviving spouse who is also a devisee
  3. Other devisees
  4. A surviving spouse
  5. Other heirs
  6. A creditor, starting 45 days after death, if the creditor follows 62-3-804(1)(b)
  7. The South Carolina Department of Revenue or a suitable person the court picks, starting four months after death

Anyone under eighteen is disqualified. When siblings disagree about who should serve, a house can sit unsold for months, so settle that early.

Informal versus formal probate

Informal probate begins with a verified application to the court. Formal testacy is a litigated proceeding started by a summons and petition. The informal application must give the applicant's interest, the decedent's name, date of death, age and domicile, and the names and addresses of the spouse, children, heirs and devisees (62-3-301). It must also state that the ten-year limit has not run.

Formal testacy decides whether a valid will was left (62-3-401). While one is pending, the court may not act on informal probate or appointment applications. A contest of an informally probated will may be brought within eight months of informal probate or one year of death, whichever is later (62-3-108(A)(2)(c)). A buyer or title company will watch that window.

Deadlines after appointment

Several clocks start at appointment, and a few start at death. These are the ones in the probate article.

Step (section)Deadline
Notice of appointment to heirs and devisees (62-3-705)Within 30 days of appointment
Inventory and appraisement (62-3-704(b), 62-3-706(A))Within 90 days of appointment
Creditor claims after published notice (62-3-801(a))Eight months after first publication
Outer limit for claims arising before death (62-3-803(a))One year after death
Pay allowed claims before closing (62-3-807(a))No later than 14 months after death, absent an extension

These clocks govern when a family can safely distribute proceeds. That is a separate question from when the house can be sold.

Can a personal representative sell the house?

Yes. The statute lets a personal representative acquire or dispose of an asset, land included, for cash or on credit, at public or private sale (62-3-715). The power begins on appointment (62-3-701), so a sale contract signed before the court issues letters stands on shaky ground.

At closing the title company will ask to see the letters, and a South Carolina deed from the estate is typically signed by the personal representative. If the estate distributes real property instead of selling it, the personal representative must execute a deed of distribution to evidence the distributee's title (62-3-907(A)). Heirs who inherit and then want out can sell afterward, but that adds a recording step.

Bond can matter too. It may be waived by affidavit when the estate's gross value is under twenty thousand dollars (62-3-603(B)(1)), and an interested person or creditor with a claim over five thousand dollars may demand one (62-3-605). Ask the probate court how it handles bond in your county.

The $45,000 small estate rule

A successor can collect personal property by affidavit when the whole probate estate, less liens and encumbrances, is worth no more than $45,000 (62-3-1201(a)). Real estate is the catch. The section governs collection of personal property, so a house usually needs a personal representative anyway.

  • Thirty days or more must have gone by since the death.
  • No application or petition for a personal representative may be pending or granted anywhere.
  • The probate judge of the decedent's county of domicile must approve and countersign the affidavit.
  • The affidavit is filed in that county's probate court.

A related summary route lets a personal representative close an estate not over $45,000 by sworn statement (62-3-1203, 62-3-1204), and the appointment ends one year after death if no claims or proceedings are pending.

How creditors are paid when the estate is short

When assets run short, claims are paid in a set order (62-3-805). The order matters if the house must be sold to cover debts.

  • Costs of administration, including attorney's fees and reasonable funeral expenses
  • Debts and taxes with preference under federal law
  • Reasonable medical, hospital and personal care costs of the last illness
  • Debts and taxes with preference under South Carolina law
  • All other claims

The personal representative publishes the creditor notice once a week for three successive weeks in a county newspaper (62-3-801(a)). A claim not presented in time is barred.

Selling an inherited house

Inherited-house sales tend to slow down at the same few points: getting letters issued, finding the original will, agreeing among heirs, and clearing back property tax or liens. Timing and habits vary by county, so call the probate court where the decedent lived before you plan around a date.

Cash Home Buyers works with personal representatives and heirs who want to sell the house as-is. We can talk before appointment, but a closing needs someone with authority to sign. Bring the death certificate, the will if there is one, and any court paperwork you already have.

What a personal representative owes the heirs

A personal representative is a fiduciary who must settle and distribute the estate under the will and the Code, as expeditiously as is consistent with the estate's best interests (62-3-703(a)). That duty reaches a house just as it reaches bank accounts. Delay that costs the estate money, such as months of carrying costs on a vacant property, is something heirs can question.

The personal representative has the same standing to sue and be sued as the decedent had before death, except for proceedings that do not survive death (62-3-703(c)). The first person issued general letters holds exclusive authority until that appointment ends or is modified (62-3-702). Acts that benefited the estate before appointment can relate back, and the personal representative may ratify acts others did for the estate (62-3-701).

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

A faster path when one heir inherits everything

If the appointed personal representative is the sole devisee or sole heir, that person may distribute the estate right after publishing the creditor notice and then file a closing statement (62-3-1203(b)). The closing statement is a verified document stating the estate was fully administered and distributed, and that a copy went to distributees and known unpaid creditors (62-3-1204(a)).

Under 62-3-301(a)(7) the court may also probate a will without appointing a personal representative. Whether that helps with a house sale depends on the title company, so ask before you list or sign anything.

Documents to gather first

Most delays come from missing paperwork. Start with this list:

  • A certified death certificate
  • The original will, if one exists, since the application must say whether the original is with the court or attached (62-3-402(a))
  • Names and addresses of the spouse, children, heirs and devisees, with ages for minors (62-3-301)
  • The current deed and a recent property tax bill
  • Mortgage statements and any lien notices

If the original will is lost, the petition must state its contents and say it is lost, destroyed or otherwise unavailable (62-3-402(a)).

Frequently asked questions

Do I need probate to sell a house in South Carolina?

Usually yes, if the house is titled only in the decedent's name. The will must be validated under 62-3-102, and a personal representative then has power to sell land under 62-3-715. Confirm your facts with the probate court.

How long does South Carolina probate take?

No single timeline applies. Deadlines include 30 days for notice to heirs, 90 days for the inventory, and eight months for creditor claims after publication. Allowed claims should be paid by 14 months after death unless extended.

Can heirs sell the house without a personal representative?

Generally not. A deed from the estate needs someone with authority. The small estate affidavit in 62-3-1201 collects personal property and does not by itself authorize a deed to land.

What is a deed of distribution?

It is the deed a personal representative signs to pass real property to a distributee, and it serves as evidence of that person's title (62-3-907(A)).

Can someone contest the will after informal probate?

Yes. A contest may be started within eight months of informal probate or one year of death, whichever is later (62-3-108(A)(2)(c)).

Is a house sale taxed as a capital gain in South Carolina?

Yes, though the state has no separate capital gains tax. A taxable gain from selling a house goes into your South Carolina income and is taxed at the regular income tax rates, after a 44 percent deduction.

Section 12-6-1150 of the S.C. Code lets individuals, estates and trusts deduct 44 percent of the net capital gain recognized in the state during the year. Net capital gain follows the federal definition in Internal Revenue Code Section 1222 and related sections.

In practice the state starts with the same gain you report to the IRS and lets you subtract 44 percent of it. Only the remaining 56 percent adds to your South Carolina taxable income.

Income tax rates on the gain

For tax years beginning after 2025, Section 12-6-510 sets a 1.99 percent rate on taxable income under $30,000. At $30,000 or more, the tax is 5.21 percent of the amount minus $966. Top-rate reductions starting with tax year 2027 depend on state revenue projections.

Wages, deductions and exemptions all change the final bill, so a tax professional should run your actual return before you sign a contract. The table lays out the pieces of the state formula.

The federal home sale exclusion

The South Carolina deduction starts from the federal net capital gain, so any gain you exclude on your federal return is not part of the gain being taxed. A single seller can shield up to $250,000 of profit on a main home, and joint filers up to $500,000.

Two tests apply. You need 24 months of ownership, and 24 months of living there, inside the five years ending on the sale date. Those months can fall at different times. A second exclusion is generally off the table if you used one on a different home sale in the previous two years.

A Form 1099-S means the sale must be reported even when the gain is fully excludable. IRS Publication 523, Selling Your Home, covers limits and exceptions to the two-year rule.

  • Lived there 2 of the last 5 years: the exclusion may apply
  • Rental or investment house: the gain is generally taxable
  • Inherited house: ask a tax professional about basis before you sell

Federal capital gains rates on top of the state tax

Federal tax on a long-term gain is separate from the South Carolina tax and is added to it. Long-term means you held the property longer than a year. Net short-term gains are taxed as ordinary income.

Federal brackets for tax years beginning in 2025 start at 0 percent. That rate covers taxable income to $48,350 for a single filer and $96,700 for joint filers. The 15 percent bracket then runs to $533,400 (single) or $600,050 (joint), with 20 percent above.

Higher investment income can also bring the net investment income tax. A South Carolina investor who sells a rental can face federal capital gains tax, that surtax and the state tax in the same year.

Selling from outside South Carolina

When the seller lives out of state, the buyer must withhold tax at closing under S.C. Code Section 12-8-580. The rate is the maximum individual rate on the gain for a nonresident individual, partnership, trust or estate, and five percent of the gain for a nonresident corporation or other entity.

If the seller hands the buyer an affidavit stating the amount of gain, withholding is figured on the gain. With no affidavit, the same rates apply to the full amount realized, and the buyer withholds all of the net proceeds if the required amount is larger.

  • Gain on a principal residence that is excluded under the federal exclusion falls outside the withholding rule.
  • The buyer must remit the withholding by the 15th day of the month after the sale month.
  • The buyer is liable for the amount. Lenders, agents and closing attorneys are not liable for collecting it but must remit what they actually withhold.
  • A seller can file an amended nonresident withholding statement to claim a refund of excess withholding.

An heir in another state who sells an inherited South Carolina house counts as a nonresident seller if the decedent lived outside the state at death. Ask the closing attorney to prepare the affidavit early so the buyer is not forced to hold back your whole check.

Closing costs that are not income tax

The deed recording fee is a transfer cost, not an income tax. It is $1.85 for each $500 of the property's value, split as $1.30 for the state and $0.55 for the county per $500. The grantor, meaning the seller, is generally liable for it.

Some deeds are exempt: deeds in lieu of foreclosure to the mortgagee, deeds on foreclosure to the mortgagee, and corrective or quitclaim deeds that confirm title already vested with no payment. On a master-in-equity sale, the buyer carries the liability instead.

Property tax gets settled at the closing table as well. Ask the county treasurer what is owed before you pick a closing date. Sumter County's Treasurer notes that real property taxes are paid one year in arrears, so the bill you owe at closing may cover the prior year.

Estates and trusts that sell a house

An estate or trust that sells a house can use the same 44 percent deduction, but only for income taxed to the estate, the trust or its individual beneficiaries. The deduction does not reach income passed through to a beneficiary that is not an individual.

If you inherited the house, your gain depends on your basis, the value used to measure profit. A CPA can confirm the basis before you sign a contract, and that number shapes how much you net from the sale.

What to gather before you call a tax professional

Collect the numbers that set your gain before you list or accept an offer. A professional can only help if the figures are in hand.

  • The purchase closing statement and the date you bought
  • Receipts for work you added, like a new roof or an addition
  • The dates you lived in the house, if you moved out
  • Depreciation you claimed, if the house was ever a rental
  • The estimated sale price and selling costs

If the house needs work, an as-is cash sale can shorten the time between the contract and the closing statement, and it skips repair bills that would otherwise change your numbers. Selling costs, the sale date and the net proceeds still affect your return, so keep every document from the closing.

Frequently asked questions

Does South Carolina have a capital gains tax?

There is no separate capital gains tax. Gains are taxed as part of South Carolina income, after a deduction of 44 percent of net capital gain under Section 12-6-1150.

What is the South Carolina income tax rate for 2026?

For tax years after 2025, the rate is 1.99 percent on taxable income under $30,000 and 5.21 percent of the amount minus $966 at $30,000 or more. Later reductions starting in 2027 depend on state revenue projections.

Can I avoid tax on selling my main house in South Carolina?

Often you can avoid much of it. The IRS excludes up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 on a joint return, when you owned and lived in the home for 24 months out of the last five years. Gain above the exclusion is still taxable.

Is there withholding if I live out of state?

Yes. The buyer withholds under Section 12-8-580, at the maximum individual rate on the gain if you give an affidavit, or on the full amount realized if you do not. Gain excluded as a principal residence is outside the rule.

Who pays the South Carolina deed recording fee?

The seller, as grantor, is generally liable for the fee of $1.85 per $500 of value, and the buyer is secondarily liable. On a master-in-equity deed the buyer pays.

Where to record a deed

The register of deeds is the office that takes deeds for the public record. Counties outside the list in SC Code 30-5-10(A) use the clerk of court, who performs the register's duties with the same powers. Berkeley and Dorchester registers serve four-year terms.

The office you need depends on where the land lies. Charleston, Greenville, Richland and Horry are among the counties with a register of deeds.

What must happen before recording

The deed has to be proved or acknowledged first, and 30-5-30 allows three routes. Use the one your closing attorney prefers.

  • A subscribing witness swears an affidavit
  • The signing follows the Uniform Recognition of Acknowledgments Act, or the signer swears the signature is theirs
  • The grantor acknowledges the deed before an officer, with two witnesses present

Deeds and mortgages executed after July 1, 1976 must carry a derivation clause and the grantee's mailing address. A clerk may not record one without the derivation clause unless the information was unavailable (30-5-35). Quitclaim and non-warranty deeds are exempt from the clause. A missing item does not by itself affect validity or record notice (30-5-35(c)).

Recording fee

Expect to pay $1.85 for every $500 of property value, rounding any fraction up to the next $500 (SC Code 12-24-10). The money divides between the state and the county.

Part of the feePer $500
State$1.30
County$0.55
Total$1.85

Of the state share, $0.10 is credited to the Heritage Land Trust Fund, $0.20 to the South Carolina Housing Trust Fund and $1.00 to the general fund (12-24-90). The county share goes to the county general fund. The register may add separate filing fees, so ask the office for its current schedule.

The fee is set by the value of the realty, determined under 12-24-30, and counted in $500 units with any fraction rounding up. Multiply the number of units by the $1.85 rate to estimate the statutory fee from your closing statement value. That arithmetic leaves out any separate filing charge the office sets.

The affidavit of value

The clerk or register must require an affidavit showing the realty's value, signed by a responsible person connected with the transaction who states that connection (12-24-70(A)(1)). The clerk may waive it at discretion. Bring the closing statement figure.

For an exempt deed, value is not required, but the affidavit must state why the deed is exempt (12-24-70(A)(2)). A willfully false affidavit is a misdemeanor with a fine up to $1,000, up to one year in prison, or both (12-24-70(C)).

Deeds exempt from the fee

Section 12-24-40 lists fifteen exemptions. Sellers run into these most:

  • Real estate worth $100 or less
  • Transfers to the federal government, a state or its political subdivisions, including school districts
  • Transfers with no gain or loss recognized under IRC Section 1041
  • Corrective or quitclaim deeds that only confirm title already vested, for no consideration
  • Deeds in lieu of foreclosure or deeds under foreclosure proceedings to the mortgagee
  • Transfers from an agent to the principal whose funds bought the realty, with a notarized document establishing the relationship

Treat any other transfer as taxable until the register says otherwise.

Timing and what you get back

The register records writings in the order they are lodged, and each must be recorded within thirty days of lodgment, with the recording bearing the lodgment date (30-5-90). The register or deputy endorses a certificate showing the time, book and page. No fee is charged for that certificate (30-5-200).

Certified copies are issued on application, with fees paid in advance if required (30-5-20). Order one after closing for your files.

Who is responsible if the fee is not collected?

Responsibility falls first on the grantor, then secondarily on the grantee (12-24-20). On master-in-equity deeds and deeds from the federal government, a state or its political subdivisions, the grantee carries the liability instead. Not paying risks a penalty of $50 to $500 per failure, and a clerk who does not collect risks the same (12-24-120).

What to bring to the register's office

Bring the original signed deed, the proof or acknowledgment, the affidavit of value or exemption, the grantee's mailing address and payment for the fee. For an estate deed, add the letters. A deed of distribution is how a personal representative passes real property to a distributee (62-3-907(A)).

A joint tenant's survivor files a certified death certificate with the register of deeds (27-7-40(b)).

Sellers working with Cash Home Buyers do not need to organize any of this alone. The closing attorney or title company usually records the deed, and we can walk you through it.

A deed lodged in the wrong county

South Carolina has a provision for transferring a recording to the correct county (30-5-100). Still, check the county before you lodge anything. A recording in the wrong place delays the sale record and can hold up your buyer's title policy.

The right county is the one where the land sits. For a house near a county line, confirm against the tax bill.

Plats and land use plans

A land development or land use plan is not required before a deed for undeveloped land, though a local entity may still require a plat when the deed is recorded (30-5-30(D)). For a lot split or a deed of part of a parcel, call the planning office in the county or city before you head to the register.

An instrument is also not denied record because the probating officer left out a service serial number (30-5-50).

Estate and foreclosure deeds

Deeds that come out of an estate or a foreclosure follow the same recording steps, with different fee treatment. A deed in lieu of foreclosure, or a deed to the mortgagee under foreclosure proceedings, is on the exemption list (12-24-40(13)). A master-in-equity deed shifts liability for the fee to the grantee (12-24-20), which matters to a buyer at a foreclosure sale.

A personal representative's deed of distribution goes through ordinary recording. For an estate deed, the register will still ask for an affidavit stating either the value or the exemption.

Why an unrecorded deed causes trouble at a sale

A buyer's title search reads the public record, and a deed that never reached the register does not appear there. Sellers who inherited a house or took title years ago sometimes find an older deed was signed but never recorded, and that has to be fixed before a clean sale. Recording is an orderly process, with deeds taken in the order lodged, so lodging the missing deed early starts that clock.

Found a gap? Ask the county's register of deeds or clerk of court what they need to accept the missing deed. A closing attorney can help sort it out.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the deed recording fee in South Carolina?

$1.85 per $500 of value or fraction, made up of $1.30 for the state and $0.55 for the county (12-24-10, 12-24-90). The office may charge separate filing fees.

Do I record at the courthouse or with the register of deeds?

The answer varies by county. In counties outside the 30-5-10(A) list, the clerk of court does the register's job.

How long does recording take?

The statute requires recording within thirty days of lodgment, in the order lodged (30-5-90).

Does a deed need witnesses in South Carolina?

Often yes. Acknowledgment before an officer is witnessed by two witnesses, but a subscribing witness affidavit is another route (30-5-30).

Do I need to record a deed at all?

Recording puts the deed in the public record where a buyer's title search will find it, and the statute sets the process once an instrument is lodged. Ask a closing attorney about priority questions.
